items.title: [ScienceDaily] Nearly 10,000 patients reveal what works best for knee arthritis pain relief
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🔭 ✏️

A major analysis of 139 clinical trials involving nearly 10,000 people suggests that some of the simplest treatments may work best for knee osteoarthritis. Knee braces ranked highest overall for reducing pain, stiffness, and mobility problems, while water-based therapy was especially effective for pain and regular exercise consistently improved both pain and physical function. More high-tech approaches, including ultrasound, generally performed worse.

items.title: [Kottke.org] A Deep Dive Into the Full Bayeux Tapestry Story
items.content_html:
From Deep Down History, an entertaining hour-long explainer video on the Bayeux Tapestry.

This video tells the Tapestry’s story in full, using Charles Stothard’s early colour reproduction, presented here as a seamless scroll for the first time. We follow Harold Godwinson’s fateful journey from Edward the Confessor’s court to Normandy, his later seizure of the Crown, and William the Conqueror’s invasion. Beyond its political messaging, the Tapestry is also bursting with medieval history, including jokes, fascinating technical details, and a warning for those who break their promises…

Completed within a decade or two of the events which it depicts, the tapestry is back in the news & public consciousness because it’s back in England for the first time since it was made and on display at the British Museum.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] A cure for physician burnout is better use of patient data
items.content_html:
🎨 🔧 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🔧 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Somewhere in America, a physician is trying to reconstruct where their patient has been for the last six months. A hospital admission in March, a discharge to a rehabilitation facility, and then the specialist follow-up that may or may not have happened, with a medication list that is out of date. The patient does their best to fill in the gaps from memory. The office visit is only 12 minutes long, and most of it is spent on detective work.

When the visit is over, the doctor returns to endless bureaucratic tasks, having spent more time digging through records and charting than caring for the patient. Members of today’s patient care continuum, like primary care, pharmacy, specialists, home health, skilled nursing, and beyond, operate on siloed, disconnected information systems that create an immense amount of inefficient work. As a result, primary care physicians spend more than half of their workday on computer-based electronic health record (EHR) tasks.

This never-ending “type‑and‑click” work is a major driver of physician burnout, which can lead to medical errors, decreased care quality, safety incidents, and reduced patient satisfaction. Some physician burnout rates are nearly 50%. The strain does not come from EHRs alone; time pressure, chaotic workplaces, low control of work pace, and organizational culture further exacerbate conditions.

In response, physicians are leaving the industry at an alarming rate. In another AMA survey, more than 35% noted interest in leaving their jobs in the next two years. The U.S. can’t stand to lose that many physicians, as the country is already projected to face a shortage of up to 86,000 physicians by 2036.

RUDDERLESS PATIENT DATA CREATES BURDEN

Health systems generate more patient data than most physicians can ever see. Unfortunately, it sits idle across disparate systems. Primary care physicians aren’t notified when one of their patients goes to the ER and requires a follow-up. A skilled nursing facility isn’t made aware of a prescription change that puts an elderly patient at risk of a dangerous medication interaction.

In our work with providers, we have found that poorly designed digital tools leave them with less time for patients and more time chasing the information they need to avoid these issues. Physicians frequently share that interoperability gaps and clunky design can affect their performance and increase patient safety risks.

One analysis found that stress from technologies, chronic time pressure, and persistent workflow issues greatly contribute to clinician burnout. Because multiple EHRs cannot easily share or interpret data, clinicians must hunt through information trails with faxes and phone calls to compile complete health pictures before making care decisions. The case for connected and actionable patient data is paramount to supporting providers’ mental health, helping them close frequent issue points, and addressing some of the main contributors to physician burnout.

SHELVE THE MINDFULNESS APPS AND PUT PATIENT DATA TO BETTER USE

People tend to categorize physician burnout as a resilience problem, something that mindfulness apps, wellness stipends, and protected lunch hours can fix. But those are band-aids. The real answer is cutting physicians’ endless hours at the keyboard by adopting technology that shares patient data among every provider who touches a patient’s care, including public health and community partners, so physicians easily understand the full health picture and receive real-time alerts on what matters most for their patients.

When data moves with the patient, each visit in the care journey changes its shape. A physician gets pinged the moment their patient lands in the hospital, knows exactly where they went after discharge, and can intercede before the next hospital readmission instead of after one. The 12-minute visit becomes 12 minutes of actual medicine instead of fatiguing detective work.

Effie Carlson is the CEO of Watershed Health and Monica Rivera, MD, MPH is the chief growth officer of Watershed Health.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] The last mile for public policy
items.content_html:
Governments ultimately deliver outcomes through thousands of people making decisions at local government, nonprofits, and service provider organizations. Technical assistance is how those decisions improve over time.

In theory, technical assistance is simple: make sure the people implementing policy know what to do, and how, with advice and guidance from state and federal agencies. It’s one of the most important aspects of how government agencies operate.

But government employees I’ve spoken with acknowledge that the status quo of how TA is delivered is fundamentally broken.

IT HAPPENS EVERY DAY

Imagine a federal program with millions of dollars in grants to disburse to state and local agencies. Before a dollar moves, program staff must define which entities are eligible, build a rubric, identify the metrics that define success and community impact, and align stakeholders across thousands of organizations nationwide. Then they must make potential grantees aware of the grant.

A significant share of that upstream work is time spent interviewing people and defining criteria. It’s careful, expensive work. And none of it matters if the dollars don’t reach the organizations that can improve the lives of the people the grant was written for.

FROM POLICY TO ACTION

Every major government initiative depends on hundreds or thousands of implementing partners from local government agencies and nonprofits to service providers.

For example, a state board of elections spends significant time advising election clerks on hiring and recruiting, advocating for rule changes with the state government, and helping educate the public about local election processes. The same is true for public health programs, veterans’ programs, homelessness coordination, and dozens of other initiatives. Technical assistance makes these programs possible, but it is delivered ad hoc, typically at a single point in time, rather than continuously meeting ongoing needs.

3 BROKEN ELEMENTS

Today’s approach to delivering technical assistance results in bottlenecks that prevent expertise from reaching the practitioners who need it when they need it.

  1. It doesn’t scale. As provider networks grow in complexity, the people with the answers become single points of failure. Professional staff burn time managing unwieldy contact lists and answering the same question repeatedly. Support becomes uneven and some organizations never get help.
  1. It falls short when it’s needed most. Service providers need technical assistance during implementation or when working through an edge case, not just at kickoff. Without current guidance, providers fall back on what they already know, which renders the upfront investment in knowledge sharing moot. Meanwhile, guidance gets buried in inboxes and shared drives, and knowledge walks out the door when a state or federal employee leaves.
  1. It’s opaque. Agency leaders struggle to see which providers are receiving assistance, how engaged partners are across the ecosystem, or where implementation is systemically breaking down. Problems surface after a missed deadline, when it is too late.

As federal policy continues to shift and states and local governments contend with budget cuts and turnover, technical assistance capacity doesn’t scale linearly with headcount.

TECHNOLOGY FOR TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE

The bulk of investment in TA programs goes to consulting engagements and professional services. Consultants have expertise and they get the content right. Where TA falls short is delivery and resilience. Without a real-time connection across the network—one that keeps knowledge from fragmenting when a contract ends—technical assistance can’t do what it’s supposed to do.

Hiring more consultants is a temporary fix. And like many state and local programs, TA runs on outdated tools and the elbow grease of already overworked public servants.

Public servants are often technologically lacking in comparison to their private sector peers, through no fault of their own. Trying to create a real-time ecosystem of people involved in TA for a program—and similar programs—requires more than listservs and spreadsheets.

Modern software that’s purpose-built for interagency collaboration, communication, and the knowledge-sharing work central to technical assistance represents a fundamental shift from a series of disconnected, point-in-time activities to lasting implementation infrastructure.

Tools built for TA must meet two requirements. First, they must capture intelligence from across the network. The answer to a question from a nonprofit employee in one county is probably useful to a local government employee on the other side of the state. Rather than remaining siloed, that knowledge bridges jurisdictional gaps and connects everyone involved in delivering a service.

Second, tools built for TA must preserve institutional memory. Instead of an answer languishing in one person’s inbox, it’s available to everyone in the ecosystem—and to everyone working on a similar initiative years from now.

Together, those two capabilities represent technical assistance as a virtuous loop. Rather than experts pushing out ad hoc information, they can see what the field is asking, provide better answers, and get sharper questions in return.

Layering AI onto the structured loop of TA data makes it possible to answer routine questions instantly while surfacing emerging implementation challenges back to program staff. Every interaction strengthens the knowledge available to the entire network.

A STANDING CAPABILITY

We must shift from treating technical assistance as a deliverable to treating it as a capability. A deliverable has a start date, an end date, and a final invoice. A capability persists. It gets stronger the more people use it, and it survives the turnover, budget cycles, and contract expirations that currently erase institutional memory every few years.

That distinction matters more now than it did five years ago. Federal requirements are shifting, budgets are volatile, and the people who know how programs work are retiring. Agencies can’t hire their way through that. But they can build a system where an answer given once is available to everyone who needs it next.

Madeleine Smith is the cofounder and CEO of Civic Roundtable.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] How to support a colleague who has lost a loved one to suicide
items.content_html:
🎨 🔧 ✏️

🎨 🔧 ✏️

🎨 🔧 ✏️

🎨 🔧 ✏️

In 2024 almost 50,000 Americans died by suicide, making it the 10th leading cause of death in the United States. And the ripple effects are even wider. According to research, each suicide is connected to 135 people who knew the deceased, including coworkers, along with a percentage of those who were considered “close connections.” Extrapolating that data, 6.6 million people are added to the larger community of suicide loss survivors each year.

I am one of those “loss survivors.” On January 5, 2025, while in a plane taxiing out on a runway, I received a text message from my half-brother telling me my father had died by suicide. The shock of his death, including how it was communicated, left me traumatized and depressed. While I was fortunate to have the strong support of my wife, daughter, and son-in-law, at some point I started to think, “Who should I tell?”

While the decision about sharing the loss of my father was highly personal and based on a number of factors, which I discussed with my grief therapist, it left me thinking, How can we support others in the workplace who have faced these unimaginable events in their lives? And that commitment is not one to be taken lightly, given the stigma of suicide, linked to effects that research lists as “concealment of the death, social withdrawal, reduced psychological and somatic functioning, and grief difficulties.”

The strategies here are designed as suggestions to help others who might want support but who might not ask for it. I would like to thank all of the mental health specialists and corporate leaders who agreed to be interviewed for this article.

I am not a mental health professional, and this is not mental health advice, but here are some approaches to your colleague who might not be ready, prepared, or equipped to share the grief and sense of loss that comes with the suicide of a loved one. 

Start with condolences

A good first step is to offer your condolences, delicately and respectfully. One person I interviewed, whose mother died by suicide, said, “A few of my colleagues handed me cards with handwritten notes of condolence. I will never forget how thoughtful that was, that they took the time to write a note of kindness.” I also experienced something similar, and will never forget those who took the time to be so mindful and respectful. Sure, email is always an option, but a deeper sense of sympathy is conveyed by a meaningful card with a handwritten note of condolences and support, beyond a simple signature.

By conveying condolences, without mentioning anything specific and respecting your colleague’s privacy, you allow the person who is grieving, as one mental health specialist stated, “to retain their own narrative without feeling like someone is being presumptive. Such gestures also convey availability and humanity without any assumption of a reply or explanation.” 

Offering further support

To gauge how to respond, you need to consider your relationship with the individual. Are they a colleague with whom you have little social connection other than work-related interactions, or a close coworker and friend you socialize with? How you decide to express your regrets should tie into that relationship.

If you don’t have a close relationship but work in the same office, a simple expression of regret or a note of support would be appreciated, demonstrating that even though you might not be particularly close, you care about your coworker and the death of their loved one. One person I interviewed told how such a work acquaintance sent a flower arrangement to their coworker’s desk, a touching gesture of support. “The fact that we were not particularly close, but he still took the time to send me some flowers, was extremely touching,” he said.

In the case of a close coworker, consider offering more support. As one corporate leader told me when such a coworker’s loved one died by suicide, “I didn’t want to just offer my condolences, I wanted to offer her my company, so I invited her to a tea outside the office, to give her a moment of respite from the stress of returning to work and to just take a break.” That invitation gave her colleague the liberty to share but without any imposition or intrusion. The corporate leader added, “My friend was just appreciative that I took her out of the office environment, and even for a brief moment, to feel that she could just converse and it didn’t have to be about her grief.”

However, keep in mind even a close colleague may not be prepared to talk about what happened. If a grieving colleague doesn’t want to engage, respect their boundaries. Especially shortly after someone’s death and the return to work,  there are strong reasons why your colleague might not want to engage more specifically, beyond accepting your condolences. Those reasons include:

  • Confusion around how the death occurred. “How could this have happened?”
  • Self-scrutiny and self-blame: “Should I have done more?”
  • Anger. “How could they have done that to us?”
  • Religious objections and guilt. 
  • Shame: “I never thought I would have this in my life.”

If your colleague does want more support 

Grief is a long and complicated journey. A colleague who may want privacy now may later approach you once they have had more time to process their grief, but only if you have conveyed your availability earlier. Here are some dos and don’ts to signal your wanting to keep the door open and render future support.  

Don’ts: These might close off any future conversations and possibilities to help.

  • Offer to talk if you don’t mean it. One person I interviewed had a colleague offer support, but when she replied months later, “Yes, I’d love to take you up on that virtual catch-up,” there was no reply. That added unnecessary hurt and isolation to what was already a difficult ask in reaching out.
  • Bring up the manner of death. A simple “If you ever want to chat and talk, just know that I am always here to support you” is empathetic while nonintrusive.
  • Make it about you. Saying something like, “I know what you are going through, the same thing happened in my family” shifts the narrative to yourself from the person you are trying to console. Worse, as one mental health professional told me, “Equating your own loss might make your colleague feel like you are minimizing theirs.” 
  • Rush in with early assurances such as, “Don’t worry, it’s going to be OK,” or, “You’re strong, you will get through it.” Your colleague is going through a period of uncertainty that needs to be understood, and empathetic listening is your best way to show support without offering what might be perceived as unhelpful counsel. 
  • Provide a reading list. There are an abundance of books on grief, some specifically pertaining to suicide. However, recommending a book can feel like an assignment, even if well intentioned. As one person I interviewed said, “It started to feel like a cascade of people offering condolences were telling me about a book that I really needed to read. It was overwhelming and also gave me anxiety as to what I should be reading, if at all.”  Recommending a book is on a very thin wire with respect to mental health counseling, so perhaps it’s not the time to signal, “Here’s what you should be doing.”

Do’s: These will signal a strong sense of future availability. 

  • If you are close to the person, and have a friendship that would be sustained even if you were not colleagues, open the door to the future. A simple “I am here if you ever want to talk,” conveys understanding and empathy, and also respects your friend’s sense of privacy. One colleague reached out to me with such an offer six months after my father’s suicide. His counsel was extremely helpful, but if he had made the offer sooner I would have been ill-prepared to accept the kind gesture. 
  • Be a steady listener. In your initial interaction with your colleague, allow them the narrative. Don’t try to finish sentences or overtake the conversation. Whatever they might share, replying with understanding and validation will demonstrate a strong sense of empathy that might be very helpful over time.
  • Offer resources, but prepare first. Many organizations offer a range of mental health support resources that can be helpful, including employee assistance programs and specific grief support and counseling access. One corporate leader explained that their company has trained mental health aides who are third-party certified to support those who are grieving. These are all helpful, but in your approach to your colleague, a good start might be, “I know we have good support and counseling resources here. If you need help finding them, or even if you want me to go to HR with you to help find where to start, just let me know.” That way, you are not overwhelming them with what might be multiple options, but just offering support without intrusion. 
  • Offer to talk outside the office. Taking someone out of the office can offer a sense of intimacy without the pressure of office interactions. With such outreach, you are offering what might be the most important thing you can offer: your undivided companionship. And it doesn’t hurt to add, “If now’s not a good time, it’s an offer with no expiry or agenda, just an excuse to get out of the office!” Sometimes a note of levity can bring a moment of relief to such an awful time. You can mention that this opportunity could be during work hours or outside them. Having a conversation after work can reduce the anxiety of feeling, “Well, we have to get back now.” 

Managers Have a Special Responsibility

When a manager has someone on their team who has experienced such a loss, the situation is different from that of a work colleague or acquaintance. As one of the corporate leaders I interviewed told me, “Managers have an obligation to intervene and offer both hard and soft resources.” 

Those could include internal and external support programs, as well as additional time off; temporary reassignment, especially if that person’s role involves travel;  and other gestures such as “What can I take off your plate right now?” 

As a mental health professional told me, “Managers are instrumental in helping to vector the person grieving to the appropriate resources, which also demonstrates a strong organizational duty of care and culture.” As studies demonstrate, a lack of “institutional care” can have a significant impact on a grieving person’s perception of support in the workplace. 

Be present, mindful, and delicate

As someone who is not a mental health professional, you can’t help another person make sense of something that makes no sense. But by being sensitive to the person’s grief in the aftermath of tragedy, you can open the door for them to reach out for companionship, comfort, and even help in finding support.  

And if that ask never comes from your colleague, as long as you were an empathetic listener, it’s not a failure on your part. After such a traumatic experience, each person’s grief narrative is different and it might or might not be something that involves workplace peers, friends, and colleagues. Yet by trying as best you can to follow these strategies, including empathetic listening and validating how your friend is coping, you can provide an opportunity for future interactions without the presumption and pressure that there might be one.  

This article does not constitute or imply mental health advice or counseling. If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, call or text 988 or visit 988lifeline.org to connect with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, available 24/7 in the United States. If there is immediate danger, call 911. People grieving a suicide loss can find support groups, peer support, and other resources at afsp.org/ive-lost-someone/.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] 25 years after 9/11, some parts of air travel are starting to look familiar again. Here’s how much flying has changed
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

It’s hard to believe that 9/11 was 25 years ago today. On that day, September 11, 2001, I was a young journalist working at CNN headquarters, producing the noon newscast, when I saw the first, and then the second, plane crash into the World Trade Center in real time on the newsroom monitor.

In an instant, everything about air travel in America changed. And 9/11 has informed the way we have traveled ever since. Gone are the days when anybody could say goodbye to loved ones at the gate. (Although that restriction has recently begun to ease; more on that below.) Also gone, for the most part: the ability to run late and still make your flight in under half an hour.

Here are a few examples of what is different between then and now.

TSA airport security checks

While there were security checks before September 11, 2001, they were nothing in comparison to the invasive TSA screening checkpoints we have today. Those screenings are a direct result of the formation of the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), which was created in November 2001, two months after the terrorist attacks.

Back then, there were no required Real IDs, no full-body screenings or mandatory metal detectors with enhanced screening technology, no need to show your ID before security, and certainly no invasive privacy measures such as facial scans employing facial recognition software.

Beyond just taking off our shoes or having to scan the contents of our carry-ons, those of us who remember long for the days when we could show up late to the gate, drink in hand, and board with relative ease.

Originally, the TSA was housed under the Department of Transportation (DOT), whose focus under the Aviation and Transportation Security Act (signed by then-President George Bush two months after the attacks) was to perform uniform, restrictive screening, and institute a federal takeover of airport security from private companies.

But in 2003, the agency moved to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Starting in 2011 with the launch of TSA PreCheck, TSA created a system that critics now argue over-screens the general public, treating every passenger as a threat instead of focusing on high-risk individuals. From body scans that employ advanced imaging technologies to restricting liquids, aerosols, and gels, airport security measures have made traveling a long, exhausting process. TSA screened 900 million people at airports in just 2025 alone.

In fact, today’s TSA’s Secure Flight program’s security measures “begin long before you arrive at the airport.” Most travelers are probably unaware that TSA screens passenger information, cross-listing it with intelligence and federal government watch lists—for both travel outside the U.S. but also within—before you even hit security.

Boarding passes

A boarding pass is now required to get to the gate. It wasn’t always. After the September 11 attacks, printed boarding passes became mandatory requirements to pass through security. By 2010, mobile boarding passes accessible from smartphones became standard.

However, this post-9/11 restriction is now starting to ease. In a welcome change for many, TSA is instituting TSA Gateside, which will ease restrictions on those who want to see off friends and family at the gate. As Fast Company previously reported, PreCheck members at select airports can now go to the gates to meet flights, even if they aren’t flying themselves.

Longer lines, even at TSA PreCheck

Since 9/11, airport wait times have occasionally averaged one to three hours at certain hubs, per NPR.

And according to a 2025 New York Times article, TSA PreCheck, which was created to cut down on the long lines formed by post-9/11 security checkpoints, doesn’t actually speed up travel by much. Reporters looked into travel at New York airports, and found PreCheck at John F. Kennedy, LaGuardia, and Newark airports only saved travelers about five to 10 minutes on average.

What travel restrictions have eased since 9/11?

Passengers have welcomed the end of the shoe removal rule, which, while not a direct result of 9/11, was also instituted around the same time.

Also expediting the security process: Some busy mothers now can access new dedicated lanes for families, as can veterans, at select airports.

items.title: [Pinterest Engineering Blog - Medium] Evolving Pinterest’s Embedding Retrieval Platform
items.content_html:
🌾 🔧 ✏️

🌾 🔧 ✏️

🌾 🔧 ✏️

🔧 ✏️

Authors: Bowen Zhou | Staff Software Engineer; Shan Gao | Senior Software Engineer; Jingwen Hu | Software Engineer II; Wenjiang Chu | Staff Software Engineer

The Billion-Embedding Challenge

At Pinterest, the “signal” is our lifeblood. Whether it’s a home decor enthusiast finding the perfect rug or a fashion seeker discovering a new aesthetic, our discovery engine relies on understanding deep semantic relationships to help our users find inspirations. Over the last few years, the explosive growth of embedding-based retrieval has fundamentally transformed how we surface these signals — and at the heart of that transformation is Manas, Pinterest’s in-house distributed search platform.

Embedding Retrieval is one of the core capabilities of Manas, supporting multiple approximate nearest neighbor search algorithms, hybrid queries with both token and embedding clauses, as well as real-time updates to ensure fresh contents become searchable within seconds. Deployed on over 80 clusters and serving billions of embeddings, Manas embedding retrieval powers all major product surfaces at Pinterest including Home Feed, Search, Related Pins, Ads, and Notifications.

However, as our corpus scales toward tens of billions of embeddings and our models capture increasingly complex interactions, we face mounting challenges around cost efficiency, scalability, and flexibility. On the infrastructure side, traditional ANN algorithms like HNSW are notoriously memory-hungry — they require the entire index to reside in RAM to maintain low query latency, making cost grow linearly with corpus size. On the modeling side, the classic two-tower retrieval paradigm is too restrictive: it reduces each candidate to a single embedding and scores relevance through a simple dot product, leaving little room to express richer, context-dependent notions of similarity.

To tackle these challenges, our team has been evolving Manas’s embedding retrieval stack across three fronts:

  • Quantization. We reduce the memory footprint of embedding indices by compressing vectors into lower-bit representations with fewer effective dimensions. Quantization has been rolled out to all major use cases, delivering over 50% memory reduction in embedding indices and 20–30% cost savings in serving infrastructure.
  • SSD-based Serving. Rather than holding entire indices in RAM, we serve ANN queries directly from SSD by carefully bounding the I/O per request — sustaining high throughput with low tail latencies at a fraction of the memory cost. Early experiments demonstrate a 10x reduction in memory usage and 40% CPU savings compared to in-memory serving
  • Multi-embedding Retrieval. We move beyond the single-vector-per-candidate constraint of the two-tower model by supporting richer scoring functions that consider multiple embeddings per candidate. This unlocks more expressive ranking at the retrieval stage. We are currently partnering with a product team to launch a pilot use case.

In this blog post, we will delve into the technical details and results of each initiative, and discuss what’s next for embedding retrieval in Manas.

Quantization: Redefining the Footprint of High-Recall Search

For a long time, serving embeddings in 16-bit or 32-bit float precision was considered the common practice. But at Pinterest’s scale, raw precision is a luxury that often provides diminishing returns. We discovered that quantization — transforming these high-dimensional float vectors into compact integer representations — is one of our most effective ways to better cost efficiency.

Evaluating the Trade-offs: SQ vs. PQ

In the Manas stack, we focused our implementation on two primary quantization algorithms: Scalar Quantization (SQ) and Product Quantization (PQ). The core of these methodologies lies in partitioning the vector space into disjoint subspaces and mapping each vector into an integer representation: SQ applies uniform discretization from float to integer per dimension, while PQ performs a K-Means clustering in each subspace and maps a subvector to the ID of the closest cluster centroid.

Benchmarks on a 100-million-embedding GraphSage dataset confirmed this intuition. We evaluated both SQ and PQ across two ANN algorithms (HNSW and IVF) and observed a clear trade-off: PQ achieves higher compression but with a significant recall decrease, while SQ delivers strong compression with minimal loss on recall.

  • PQ reduces the HNSW index by 74% and the IVF index by 93%, with a recall in the range of 70–80%
  • SQ reduces the HNSW index by 59% and the IVF index by 75%, with a recall over 90% consistently

Given the trade-off demonstrated by the offline benchmarking exercise, we ran online A/B experiments in production to select the best performing quantizer for each use case, and ensure negligible impact on user engagement metrics when enabling quantization. We launched SQ and PQ across major product use cases, reducing the total memory allocation significantly and realizing 20–30% cost savings for serving.

Technical Deep Dive: SIMD and Linear Scaling

Shifting to 8-bit or 4-bit representations isn’t just a memory win; it’s a compute challenge. Usually, SQ requires a decoding step before distance computation, which can become a CPU bottleneck. To solve this, we implemented Linear Scaling SQ, which quantizes a vector by scaling only, and thus eliminates the decoding step before distance computation. The key enabler here is SIMD intrinsics, which allows the CPU to perform multiple 8-bit integer operations with each instruction, and hence reduces the total computing resources needed per query by 10–15% in our use cases.

SSD Serving: Moving Beyond the Constraints of RAM

Our journey of improving embedding retrieval cost efficiency led us to exploring alternative ANN algorithms that take advantage of recent NVMe SSD performance advancements. The current generation of SSD devices are roughly an order of magnitude cheaper per gigabyte, but with the latency increased from nanoseconds to microseconds, which can slow down queries if I/O operations are not carefully managed. To bridge this gap, we experimented with I/O-aware ANN algorithms that were designed to minimize the number of random reads issued per query while retaining a recall score as good as memory-based algorithms.

DiskANN vs. SPANN

In our experiments, we benchmarked two disk-based ANN algorithms, DiskANN and SPANN, with a 100M-embedding corpus collected from a Pinterest Search use case. While DiskANN is a robust graph-based approach, SPANN emerged as the better option for the Manas use cases.

Our team’s key observation was applying PQ quantization to the on-disk embedding store while retaining the full precision centroids helped the search accuracy and throughput significantly — a slight tweak from the original SPANN paper. This makes SPANN+PQ 4.5x faster than plain SPANN and achieves over 3x the QPS of DiskANN with 1/3 the latency, with a slight 5% recall drop.

Implementing SPANN in Manas

We implemented the SPANN algorithm in Manas, which stores the centroid index in the memory and the large posting lists in the disk, and guarantees both disk-access efficiency (low latency) and high recall by effectively reducing the disk access number per request. In the index-building stage, we adopt the hierarchical balanced clustering algorithm from SPANN for selecting the centroids, which ensures evenly distributed cluster sizes, and hence similar lengths of posting lists to keep the tail latency low. We build the centroid index using HNSW, which is well-suited for in-memory search over a relatively small set of centroids. In a preliminary evaluation with a Pin recommendation use case that indexes over 5 billion embeddings, our SPANN implementation saves over 40% of CPU time for production queries when compared with HNSW, with a <5% recall drop. Our next step is to adopt SPANN across all major use cases.

Multi-Embedding Retrieval: The Shift Toward Late Interaction

As we improve cost efficiency, we are also evolving the expressivity of the Manas embedding retrieval stack. The traditional “Two-Tower” model, while efficient, collapses an entire Pin or query into a single vector, often losing the nuanced, token-level semantics that define high-quality discovery.

Contrast in Paradigms: Sum of MaxSim

We are now moving toward Late Interaction models , such as ColBERT. Unlike the single dot product of two-tower models, late interaction represents documents and queries as lists of vectors. We use the “Sum of MaxSim” scoring logic to capture the maximum similarity between each query token and the document’s tokens.

Integrating this into Manas required comprehensive changes in our serving stack. We integrated the multi-embedding retrieval as a new query type and updated Manas to handle multiple query embeddings rather than a single vector per query. This required updating the Manas query parser to understand these complex queries, as well as running multiple ANN searches from a multi-embedding query simultaneously. Currently, we are working with a client team to launch a pilot use case for the multi-embedding query support in Manas. This represents the next frontier of Pinterest search: moving from “two tower” to true model-based retrieval.

Looking Ahead

The future of vector search at Pinterest lies at the intersection of infrastructure efficiency and retrieval model innovation. Over the next five years, our central goal is to evolve Manas embedding retrieval into an architecture that is scalable, cost-efficient, and open to new retrieval paradigms. We are pursuing this along three directions: adopting SPANN and SPFresh to push CPU and memory costs even lower for billion-scale indices; building first-class support for multi-embedding retrieval models like ColBERT that enable richer, interaction-based scoring at the retrieval stage; and embracing GPU-based retrieval systems like SilverTorch and TIGER to unlock new model capabilities.

Acknowledgements

Many people from Core and Ads Delivery Infra teams contributed to the projects discussed in this blog post. Special thanks to Ellie Madsen, Jennifer Kong, and Jiawei Kuang for working on various Manas embedding retrieval projects. Thanks to our collaborators from client teams, including Bowen Deng, Jiaxing Qu, Ryan Hou, Minhazul Islam SK, Wei-Ting Lin, J.J. Hu, Konik Kothari, Yujiao Guo, Hanlin Lu, Bella Huang, Ai Zhang, Janvi Palan. Last but not least, many thanks to Van Lam, Tao Yang, Deeksha Sharma, Kartik Paramasivam, Abhishek Tayal, Zheng Liu for leadership support.

Evolving Pinterest’s Embedding Retrieval Platform was originally published in Pinterest Engineering Blog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] AI isn’t replacing jobs; it’s restructuring work
items.content_html:
🎨 🔧 🪶 🌲 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🔧 🪶 🌲 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🔧 🪶 🌲 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🔧 🪶 🌲 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🔧 🪶 🌲 🔭 ✏️

Companies are racing to automate work without realizing they may also be automating away the systems that create expertise. That is the workforce challenge emerging beneath today’s AI conversation.

Most debates focus on whether AI will replace jobs. But jobs are the wrong lens for this discussion.

Work has always been made up of tasks, decisions, workflows, and capabilities bundled together under a title and scope. What AI is doing quite efficiently is unbundling that structure and redistributing the work itself. That changes how organizations create value. And it fundamentally changes how leaders should think about workforce strategy.

AI reshapes career ladders

ADP Research has been studying how AI is reshaping work in collaboration with researchers at the Stanford Digital Economy Lab. One of the clearest signals emerging is that the impact of AI is not evenly distributed across organizations. While experienced workers may have anticipated disruption, in practice, many organizations are seeing something more nuanced.

AI performs exceptionally well against structured, repeatable, and rules-based work. Historically, that has often been the work assigned to junior employees. It is where people learn to build repetitions, pattern recognition, and operational judgment.

More experienced professionals tend to operate in environments where context, interpretation, and synthesis matter more. AI can accelerate that work, but it does not fully replace it. In many cases, expertise becomes more valuable in an AI-enabled environment because experienced workers know how to direct, evaluate, and refine machine output.

Experience becomes a multiplier, and that creates a more complicated workforce challenge than many organizations realize.

Erosion at the bottom

The real risk may not be displacement at the top of the organization, but erosion at the bottom.

Business leaders are already beginning to recognize the scale of this challenge as companies invest in upskilling workers to meet the changing nature of job roles and responsibilities. Yet upskilling alone doesn’t answer a more fundamental question: if AI increasingly performs the work where those capabilities were historically developed, how do organizations create the next generation of expertise?

Entry-level work has always served two functions simultaneously: generating operational output and developing future expertise. But as AI assumes more of the repetitive work that once served as a training ground, organizations need new ways to develop the judgment, pattern recognition, and decision-making capabilities that experience has historically created.

When organizations automate too much of that foundational layer too quickly, they risk weakening the long-term capability pipeline enterprises depend on. The challenge is no longer simply workforce automation; it is workforce architecture.

These questions will define the next generation of workforce strategy:

  • How do organizations develop judgment when traditional learning pathways disappear?
  • How do companies build expertise when repetitive work—historically the training ground for future leaders—is increasingly handled by machines?
  • How do enterprises redesign work without unintentionally constraining future talent development?

Answering these questions—not simply deploying AI faster—will separate organizations that build durable talent pipelines from those that quietly hollow them out.

From roles to capabilities

The implications extend well beyond hiring. As work becomes increasingly task-oriented and capability-based, traditional job descriptions become less meaningful than the capabilities individuals can apply across different contexts. Organizations are beginning to shift from static role structures toward capability systems built around a clear-eyed view of what skills exist inside the enterprise, which capabilities are increasing in value, and which activities should remain human-led. The work also requires understanding where AI enhances productivity versus where it introduces risk, and how human and machine work should be orchestrated together.

That transition affects nearly every workforce system: talent development, workforce planning, mobility, compensation, performance evaluation, organizational design, and leadership development. The future of workforce strategy is becoming less about managing roles and more about designing capability ecosystems.

Data as strategic visibility

Historically, payroll and workforce systems were viewed primarily through an administrative lens. But workforce data increasingly provides visibility into how work is performed across organizations: where expertise is concentrated, how workflows operate, where friction exists, and how value moves through the enterprise.

For organizations navigating AI transformation, that visibility becomes strategic.

Companies that understand how work flows through their organizations will redesign faster and more intelligently than those relying on static org charts and outdated role structures.

At the same time, enterprise leaders must recognize that AI adoption inside workforce systems operates differently than consumer AI experimentation.

HR, payroll, benefits, workforce compliance, and employee systems are deeply interconnected, compliance-driven environments. Accountability cannot disappear simply because software becomes more capable.

This is why the future of enterprise AI will not simply be defined by automation. It will be defined by orchestration: where human oversight remains necessary, how accountability is maintained, how workflows are redesigned responsibly, and how organizations preserve trust while increasing efficiency.

While consumer AI optimizes convenience, enterprise AI must optimize accountability. That distinction will shape the next generation of workforce systems.

Redesign work intentionally

Companies succeeding with AI are not treating it purely as a productivity tool. They are redesigning work intentionally. They are using AI to remove friction while elevating human contribution toward high-value activities: interpretation, relationship management, creativity, judgment, and strategic decision-making.

The future of work is not humans versus AI. It is about understanding which systems, decisions, and capabilities are best handled by machines and which remain fundamentally human. The organizations that approach this transition thoughtfully will create stronger, more adaptive workforce models.

The organizations that pursue automation without redesign risk weakening the very capabilities they will depend on most in the future. As leaders rethink work for the AI era, the most important question may no longer be, “What can AI automate?” but “How do we continue developing the human capabilities that organizations will depend on most?” The companies that answer that question well won’t just adopt AI more successfully—they have the potential to build stronger, more resilient organizations for the long term.

Usman “Oz” Khan is senior vice president of ADP Ventures.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] It took 2,977 drones to create this stunning 9/11 memorial show. Here’s how they pulled it off
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 ✏️

🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 ✏️

🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 ✏️

🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 ✏️

🎨 🔧 🪶 🌲 ✏️

To remember the lives of the 2,977 people killed in the 9/11 attacks 25 years ago, 2,977 drones were arranged in the shape of the original Minoru Yamasaki-designed World Trade Center at full architectural scale for a stunning temporary memorial. It took a lot of planning to make it work.

Called “2,977 Lights Over New York Harbor,” the commemorative public art installation on September 9 was sponsored by the New York Foundation for the Arts, and pulling it off required coordination with dozens of agencies. One of the biggest challenges was finding a suitable launch location.

“We need a lot of space to set the drones down,” Kyle Pivnick, vice president of Texas-based Sky Elements Drones, tells Fast Company, noting that thousands of hours went into finding the right path to bring the memorial to life.

The installation was produced by Sky Elements (which has put on professional drone shows for Formula 1 and Lollapalooza) in partnership with creative director Addison Mehr, Studio Drift, Ideko, designer Yan Paul Dubbelman, and artistic advisers Shigeru Ban and Dean Maltz, with input from 9/11 families, survivors, and first responders.

The installation’s creators needed about 12,000 square feet of flat, open-sky ground, which isn’t easy to find in New York City. Eventually, the U.S. Coast Guard agreed to let the creators use a parking lot at its recruitment office on the southern tip of Manhattan as the staging area.

The show was held for just one night, and it required flight restrictions so there would be no air traffic in the area, as well securing the ground below from people and moving vehicles, which is why it was held over the waterfront instead of the original World Trade Center location.

Using exactly 2,977 drones, one for each life lost at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and the United Airlines crash site in Pennsylvania on September 11, 2001, was foundational to the project. But that meant being deliberate about where to fill and add detail when re-creating the Twin Towers, Pivnick says.

“More drones would of course be better to give the towers more detail, but the choice to keep the drone count at 2,977 was paramount,” he says.

Drone shows are popular for advertising or entertainment events, but for “2,977 Lights Over New York Harbor,” the goal was to create an experience that was reverent and respectful.

The drones first appeared like two upward-swirling helixes before slowly rearranging into the shape of the towers. The helix shape was meant to recall the unbuilt proposal for a World Cultural Center memorial designed by Think that featured two open latticework towers.

By re-creating the towers as tall as they once stood, the installation gave a sense of scale and a feeling that’s larger than life. By using exactly 2,977 drones, the remembrance was poignant and personal.
